title: What is the self? Six darśanas and three Vedāntas
subject: concept:atman
question: What is the self (ātman / puruṣa / jīva), how many selves are there, and is consciousness its essence?

rows.statement: The self (puruṣa) exists because aggregates serve another, someone must experience and oversee, and activity aims at isolation; selves are many, since birth, death and faculties are allotted to each separately; the self is a witness, isolated, indifferent, a seer and not an agent.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

rows.statement: The self is the seer, pure seeing only; though pure it beholds the mind’s contents; in the stilled mind the seer abides in its own nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: The self is known by its marks — desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition — so cognition is a quality the self has, not its nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Breath, blinking, life, mental motion, sense-modification, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort are marks of the self; selves are many because their situations differ.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Against those who deny a self, Śabara argues that “we apprehend the self through desire”, since one desires only what one has experienced before — the self is a lasting experiencer who reaps the fruits of ritual acts.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: The individual self is in reality identical with brahman, pure consciousness; its apparent individuality and agency arise from superimposition and ignorance.
Selves are real, eternal and many; together with matter they are the body of brahman, which “has everything as its body” — distinct as a body from its soul, yet inseparable.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

rows.statement: The difference of selves from God and from one another is real and eternal; selves are dependent on Viṣṇu, who alone is independent.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Dvaita.net input via GRETIL)

rows.statement: Selves belong to the Lord’s marginal (taṭasthā) energy, one with and different from him in an inconceivable way.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

note: Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā all hold that selves are many and eternal but disagree on whether consciousness is the self’s essence (Sāṅkhya–Yoga) or a quality it acquires (Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika). The three Vedāntas then disagree on the self’s relation to brahman: identity, body–soul inseparability, or eternal difference. The rows are not harmonised.

title: How is brahman related to the world?
subject: concept:brahman
question: Is the world real, and how does it relate to brahman?

rows.statement: Brahman is that from which the origin, maintenance and dissolution of this world proceed; the effect is non-different from the cause, “as shown by the word ārambhaṇa and others”; creation is mere play, as in the world.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

rows.statement: Duality is mere māyā; non-duality is the highest truth; nothing is ever originated — “no self is born”.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)
sources.quote: na kaścij jāyate jīvaḥ saṃbhavo 'sya na vidyate

rows.statement: Śaṅkara reads “non-different” as: the effect has no reality apart from the cause; the manifold world is a product of name and form projected by ignorance, real only from the empirical standpoint.
Brahman really transforms into the world (pariṇāma); difference and non-difference are both real, the difference of selves being due to limiting adjuncts.
The world is real and is brahman’s body; Rāmānuja rejects the Advaita view that brahman itself is ignorant and wanders in saṃsāra, and judges bhedābheda even worse.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

rows.statement: The world is real (“satyaṃ ca jagad īdṛśam”); the stream of the world, endowed with five differences, is real, and the five differences are eternal.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Dvaita.net input via GRETIL)

rows.statement: The world and selves are naturally (svābhāvika) both different and non-different from brahman, as effects from a cause and parts from a whole.
Brahman becomes the world without itself changing (avikṛta-pariṇāma); the world is real and “pure”, untouched by māyā.

The world is the real product of the Lord’s external (bahiraṅgā) energy; energies are one with and different from their possessor in a way that is inconceivable — “inconceivability is the making-possible of the impossible”.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

note: All schools comment on the same sūtras (BS 1.1.2; 2.1.14) yet disagree on whether the world is an appearance (Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara), a real transformation (Bhāskara, Vallabha), the body of brahman (Rāmānuja), or a real, dependent and different reality (Madhva).

title: Why is the Veda authoritative — or is it?
subject: col:vedic-samhitas
question: On what ground, if any, is the Veda a valid means of knowledge?

rows.statement: Dharma is known by Vedic injunction; the word–meaning relation is original, so the Veda is an independent authority needing nothing else; names like Kāṭhaka mark expounders, not authors.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)
GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

rows.statement: Perception grasps only what is present; inference, comparison and postulation are based on perception and so cannot reveal dharma either — only the Veda can.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: The Veda is valid like spells and medicine, “because of the validity of the reliable speaker” (āpta) — authority derives from a trustworthy author.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: The authority of the Veda follows from its being “his” word; the composition of sentences in the Veda presupposes intelligence.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Vedic ritual means are “like the visible means” — impure, marked by decay and excess; reliable testimony is a means of knowledge for what is beyond perception and inference.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)
sources.quote: dṛṣṭavad ānuśravikaḥ sa hy a-viśuddhi kṣayā'tiśaya-yuktaḥ

rows.statement: Testimony (āgama) is one of three means of valid knowledge, with perception and inference.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Brahman is the source of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures, which only an omniscient being could produce; and brahman is known only through scripture.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: Lokāyata is counted with Sāṅkhya and Yoga as a form of investigative reasoning; later doxographies present the Cārvākas as rejecting Vedic authority altogether.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Kangle’s edition, 2nd ed. Bombay 1969)

note: Mīmāṃsā makes the Veda authoritative because it has no author; Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika because it has a reliable (for later Nyāya, divine) author; Advaita because brahman is both its source and its sole object. Sāṅkhya accepts testimony but devalues Vedic ritual. Not harmonised.

title: What is liberation, and how is it reached?
subject: concept:moksha
question: What is the highest goal according to each school, and what brings it about?

rows.statement: No self is bound or released; prakṛti is. From practice of the principles arises the complete knowledge “I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I”; the knower lives on like a spinning potter’s wheel, and at death attains final, absolute isolation (kaivalya).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)
sources.quote: nā 'smi na me nā 'ham ity a-pariśeṣam

rows.statement: Unwavering discriminative insight is the means of release; kaivalya is the return of the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, or the power of consciousness established in its own nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Release (apavarga) follows the successive removal of false knowledge, faults, activity, birth and suffering; it is absolute freedom from suffering.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Dharma brings prosperity and the highest good; mokṣa is the absence of conjunction (of self and body) and of further birth once the unseen force is spent.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: The inquiry concerns dharma, the purpose known by injunction; the Sūtra’s concern is the fruit of rites (e.g. heaven), and liberation became a Mīmāṃsā theme only with later authors such as Kumārila.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

rows.statement: Knowledge of brahman, whose fruit is the highest good, depends on no further act; ritual results are impermanent (CU 8.1.6 quoted); the qualified seeker needs discrimination, detachment, calm and desire for release.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: Liberation is attained by meditative devotion (bhakti) grounded in knowledge and by the Lord’s grace; the released self enjoys brahman’s bliss in its own distinct form.
Viṣṇu is the object of the inquiry; one is released only through his grace (prasāda), which follows the knowledge arising from inquiry.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Liberation comes from knowing the five differences, Viṣṇu’s faultlessness and the excellence of his qualities — “and not otherwise”.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Dvaita.net input via GRETIL)
sources.quote: pañcabhedāṃ śca vijñāya viṣṇoḥ svābhedameva ca

rows.statement: The highest goal is loving devotion (prema) to Kṛṣṇa, savoured as a rasa, which the Gauḍīyas place above liberation itself.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

note: The schools differ on whether liberation is isolation of consciousness (Sāṅkhya–Yoga), cessation of suffering (Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika), realised identity (Advaita), or loving communion by grace (theistic Vedānta). Not harmonised.

title: How Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and Madhva read Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1–4
subject: psg:bs-1-1-1-4
question: What do “then, therefore” (1.1.1) and “because scripture is its source” (1.1.3) mean, and what is the brahman being inquired into?

rows.statement: athāto brahmajijñāsā — janmādyasya yataḥ — śāstrayonitvāt — tat tu samanvayāt (the bare sūtras, open to all readings).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

rows.statement: “Then” means after the fourfold qualification, not after the study of ritual: inquiry into brahman is possible even before inquiry into dharma. 1.1.3 has two senses: brahman is the source of the Veda, and brahman is known only through the Veda.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))
GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: “Then” means after acquiring knowledge of works (the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā): the two Mīmāṃsās form one śāstra. Brahman is the highest Person, free from all imperfection, with infinite auspicious qualities; the long “great discussion” on this sūtra refutes Advaita’s attributeless brahman and its doctrine of ignorance.

The Sūtra was composed by Hari as Vyāsa at the request of Brahmā, Śiva and others; brahman is Nārāyaṇa, “whose sole body is the fullness of qualities”, the meaning of Om and of all the Veda; the inquiry leads to release through his grace.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

note: Śaṅkara detaches Vedānta from prior ritual study; Rāmānuja binds Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā into one discipline; Madhva makes the Sūtra Viṣṇu’s own revelation. The Śrībhāṣya row relies on Thibaut’s translation because the GRETIL Śrībhāṣya file could not be retrieved.

title: How many means of valid knowledge?
subject: concept:pramana
question: Which pramāṇas does each school accept?

rows.statement: Three: perception, inference and reliable testimony, since all other means are included in these.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

rows.statement: Three: perception, inference and testimony (āgama).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Four: perception, inference, comparison (upamāna) and verbal testimony.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Vaiśeṣika recognises two, perception and inference, treating testimony and comparison as forms of inference.
Śabara names perception, inference, comparison, postulation (arthāpatti) and verbal testimony, and treats absence (abhāva) as well.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts five, rejecting non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) as a separate means.
Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā accepts six: perception, inference, testimony, comparison, postulation and non-apprehension; Advaita later adopts the same six.
The Lokāyata, here a branch of ānvīkṣikī, is known from later sources as accepting perception alone.

title: When does a son acquire ownership of family property?
subject: concept:daya
question: Do heirs own ancestral property from birth, or only on the owner’s death?

rows.statement: After the death of father and mother the brothers, coming together, should divide the paternal estate equally, “for they have no power over it while the two are alive”.

sources.quote: bhajeran paitṛkaṃ riktham anīśās te hi jīvatoḥ

rows.statement: In land acquired by the grandfather, a corporate holding or movables, the ownership of father and son is equal.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Mitākṣarā text, ed. N. R. Acharya, Bombay 1949)
sources.quote: tatra syāt sadṛśaṃ svāmyaṃ pituḥ putrasya caiva hi

rows.statement: Ownership is a matter of worldly usage, and “in the world the ownership of sons and others by birth itself is well established”; partition only divides what is already jointly owned.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text
sources.quote: loke ca putrādīnāṃ janmanaiva svatvaṃ prasiddhataraṃ nāpahnavam arhati

rows.statement: Sons acquire ownership only on the father’s death (or fall or renunciation); until then the father is sole owner and may dispose even of ancestral property.

note: Colonial courts applied the Mitākṣarā outside Bengal and the Dāyabhāga in Bengal; the Manu row is earlier than both and is cited by each in its own way.

title: Are the āśramas alternatives or stages?
subject: concept:ashrama
question: How do the Dharma Sūtras present the orders of life?

rows.statement: There are four āśramas — householder, residence at the teacher’s house, the silent ascetic and the forest-dweller; living in any of them as taught, one reaches peace.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on Bühler’s edition (3rd ed. 1932); praśna.paṭala.khaṇḍa.sūtra numbering)
sources.quote: catvāra āśramā gārhasthyam ācārya.kulaṃ maunaṃ vānaprasthyam iti

rows.statement: Some allow a choice among the āśramas; but the teachers hold that there is only one, because householdership is directly enjoined in the Veda.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on Gokhale’s edition, Pune 1910 (Stenzler numbering))
GRETIL e-text (based on Gokhale’s edition, Pune 1910 (Stenzler numbering))

rows.statement: The teachers hold there is a single āśrama, because the others do not produce offspring.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: One may renounce directly from studentship, from the household or from the forest — renunciation need not wait for the later stages.

note: Olivelle (1993) reads these passages as evidence that the āśramas were originally alternative lifelong vocations, later reorganised into the sequential “four stages”.
